tldr: LLaMA trains a family of 7B–65B parameter foundation models exclusively on publicly available data and shows that a smaller model trained longer is cheaper at inference while matching or beating GPT-3 175B and Chinchilla 70B on most benchmarks.
overview: Touvron et al. (2023) introduce LLaMA, a suite of openly released foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters, all trained solely on publicly available text (CommonCrawl, C4, GitHub, Wikipedia, Books, ArXiv, StackExchange — roughly 1.4T tokens). The central finding is that Chinchilla-optimal training budget allocations favour larger models, but inference budgets favour smaller models trained longer: LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 175B on most standard benchmarks despite being 10x smaller. The architecture is a standard transformer with three targeted improvements adopted from recent work: pre-normalization using RMSNorm, SwiGLU activation functions, and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) in place of absolute position embeddings. Training efficiency is achieved via FlashAttention-style causal attention, activation checkpointing, and tensor/sequence parallelism across 2048 A100-80GB GPUs.

sections.title: Abstract & 1. Introduction
sections.summary: Motivates the inference-budget perspective on scaling: given a fixed performance target, a smaller model trained longer than compute-optimal is cheaper to serve. LLaMA-13B beats GPT-3 175B on most benchmarks; LLaMA-65B is competitive with Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B. All models are released publicly.

sections.title: 2.1 Pre-training Data
sections.summary: Training uses seven publicly available sources: English CommonCrawl (67%), C4 (15%), GitHub (4.5%), Wikipedia (4.5%), Gutenberg and Books3 (4.5%), ArXiv (2.5%), and StackExchange (2%). The total tokenized dataset is approximately 1.4T tokens; most tokens are seen only once, with Wikipedia and Books seen roughly twice.

sections.title: 2.2 Architecture
sections.summary: Standard autoregressive transformer with three modifications: RMSNorm for pre-normalization (training stability, from GPT-3 practice), SwiGLU activation with dimension 2/3 * 4d instead of 4d (from PaLM), and rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) replacing absolute embeddings (from GPTNeo/RoFormer). Model sizes range from 6.7B to 65.2B parameters.

sections.title: 2.3 Optimizer
sections.summary: AdamW optimizer with beta1=0.9, beta2=0.95, cosine learning rate schedule decaying to 10% of the peak, weight decay 0.1, gradient clipping 1.0, and 2000 warmup steps. Batch size and learning rate are varied by model size as detailed in Table 2.

sections.title: 2.4 Efficient Implementation
sections.summary: Uses an efficient causal multi-head attention implementation (xformers library, inspired by FlashAttention) that avoids storing attention weights and skips masked key/query scores. Activation checkpointing saves expensive linear layer outputs to reduce recomputed activations during the backward pass. At 65B scale, training processes ~380 tokens/sec/GPU and takes approximately 21 days on 2048 A100-80GB GPUs.

sections.title: 3. Main Results
sections.summary: Evaluates zero-shot and few-shot across 20 benchmarks covering common sense reasoning, closed-book QA, reading comprehension, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and MMLU. LLaMA-65B matches or beats Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B on most tasks; LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 on most benchmarks despite being 10x smaller.

sections.title: 3.1 Common Sense Reasoning
sections.summary: Zero-shot results on eight benchmarks (BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e, ARC-c, OBQA). LLaMA-65B surpasses Chinchilla-70B on all but BoolQ and beats PaLM-540B on all but BoolQ and WinoGrande.

sections.title: 3.2 Closed-Book Question Answering
sections.summary: Zero-shot and few-shot exact match on NaturalQuestions and TriviaQA. LLaMA-65B achieves state-of-the-art in closed-book settings on both; LLaMA-13B is competitive with GPT-3 and Chinchilla despite being 5-10x smaller and running on a single V100 at inference.

sections.title: 3.3 Reading Comprehension
sections.summary: Zero-shot accuracy on RACE (middle and high school). LLaMA-65B scores 67.9 on RACE-middle and 51.6 on RACE-high, competitive with PaLM-540B; LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 by a few points.

sections.title: 3.4 Mathematical Reasoning
sections.summary: Evaluated on MATH and GSM8k. LLaMA-65B outperforms Minerva-62B on GSM8k (20.5 vs. 43.4 with majority voting at k=100) without any mathematical fine-tuning; quantitative reasoning remains a relative weakness compared to fine-tuned specialist models.

sections.title: 3.5 Code Generation
sections.summary: Evaluated on HumanEval and MBPP. LLaMA-13B outperforms LaMDA 137B on both; LLaMA-65B (pass@1 = 23.7 on HumanEval) outperforms PaLM-62B. Performance trails code-specific fine-tuned models but is strong for a general-purpose model.

sections.title: 3.6 Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU)
sections.summary: Five-shot accuracy: LLaMA-65B scores 63.4% average, behind Chinchilla-70B (67.5%) and PaLM-540B (69.3%). The authors attribute the gap to LLaMA using limited book and academic paper data (~177GB vs. up to 2TB) in pre-training.

sections.title: 3.7 Evolution of Performance During Training
sections.summary: Most benchmarks improve steadily with training tokens and correlate with perplexity. SIQA shows high variance (considered unreliable); WinoGrande performance is similar for LLaMA-33B and LLaMA-65B throughout training.

sections.title: 4. Instruction Finetuning
sections.summary: A brief instruction-tuning experiment (LLaMA-I, same protocol as Flan) boosts MMLU from 63.4% to 68.9% for the 65B model, outperforming other moderate-size instruction-tuned models, though still below GPT code-davinci-002 at 77.4%.

sections.title: 5. Bias, Toxicity and Misinformation
sections.summary: Evaluates on RealToxicityPrompts, CrowS-Pairs, WinoGender, and TruthfulQA. Toxicity increases with model size (especially on Respectful prompts); CrowS-Pairs bias is comparable to GPT-3 and OPT-175B. TruthfulQA scores are higher than GPT-3 but still reflect hallucination risk.

sections.title: 6. Carbon Footprint
sections.summary: Training the full LLaMA model family consumed an estimated 2,638 MWh, emitting approximately 1,015 tCO2eq under US average carbon intensity. By contrast OPT-175B required 356 MWh and BLOOM-175B 475 MWh; LLaMA-7B alone required only 36 MWh.

sections.title: 7. Related Work & 8. Conclusion
sections.summary: Situates LLaMA in the history of language model scaling and open-source LLMs (OPT, BLOOM, GPT-NeoX). The conclusion reaffirms that state-of-the-art performance is achievable with only public data, and signals intent to release larger models and to explore instruction tuning more deeply.

readingFocus: The inference-budget argument: why training a smaller model longer beats training a larger model to compute-optimal — this reframes the Chinchilla scaling law for deployment contexts relevant to Microlab's Phase 3 efficiency work.

The three architecture modifications (RMSNorm pre-normalization, SwiGLU activation, RoPE) and why each was chosen — these are now standard in most open LLMs and are the architectural baseline for Phases 3-5 experiments.
The data mixture proportions and filtering pipeline (CCNet, deduplication, language ID) — directly informs how to construct and document a pretraining dataset for Phase 3.

The FlashAttention-style efficient attention and activation checkpointing — the techniques behind the 380 tokens/sec/GPU throughput figure and key to understanding memory-efficient training in Phase 4.

The MMLU gap (63.4% vs. Chinchilla 67.5%) traced to book/academic data volume — a concrete example of how data composition, not just size, drives benchmark performance, relevant to eval harness interpretation in Phase 5.
